title: CORS Best Practices and Troubleshooting
description: Learn production-ready CORS patterns and how to diagnose and fix common CORS errors.

data.text: CORS is a security boundary, not just a configuration checkbox. Following these practices keeps your API safe while still allowing legitimate frontend applications to work.

items.text: Never use AllowAnyOrigin() in production — it defeats the purpose of CORS
items.hint: AllowAnyOrigin allows every website on the internet to call your API.

items.text: Pair AllowCredentials() with WithOrigins() and explicit domain names
items.hint: AllowAnyOrigin and AllowCredentials together cause a runtime CORS error.

items.text: Use HTTPS origins only in WithOrigins()
items.hint: Browsers block mixed-content requests from HTTPS pages to HTTP origins.

items.text: Apply the most restrictive policy that still works
items.hint: Start with a narrow allowlist and expand only when needed.

items.text: Place app.UseCors() after UseRouting and before UseAuthorization()
items.hint: CORS must run before authorization so the browser preflight is handled correctly.

items.text: Do not use CORS as a replacement for authentication or authorization
items.hint: CORS is a browser-enforced convenience; server-side auth is still required.

cards.title: Development
cards.description: Local development usually runs the frontend and API on different ports.
pros: Fast iteration without managing domain lists
cons: Should be replaced with a real allowlist before production

cards.title: Production
cards.description: Production APIs should restrict access to known origins only.
pros: Prevents unauthorized websites from using your API
cons: Requires maintaining a list of allowed origins
New frontend domains need explicit approval

data.text: The browser console is your best friend when debugging CORS. Below are the most common errors and their typical fixes.

rows: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource
The server did not enable CORS for this endpoint
Register and apply a CORS policy in Program.cs
The value of the 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header in the response must not be the wildcard '*' when the request's credentials mode is 'include'
Replace AllowAnyOrigin with WithOrigins and explicit domains
Request header field Authorization is not allowed by Access-Control-Allow-Headers
The preflight response did not include the header
Method POST is not allowed by Access-Control-Allow-Methods
The policy did not allow the HTTP method
CORS preflight channel did not succeed
The OPTIONS request returned a non-2xx status or the route was not matched
Ensure UseCors is placed after UseRouting and before UseAuthorization

data.title: Debug Tip
data.text: Always inspect the Network tab in browser DevTools. Look at the OPTIONS request first: check its response status and response headers. The actual failing request will usually have a CORS error only because the preflight already failed.

A common misunderstanding is treating CORS as a security wall. It is not. CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server. Any server-side client (curl, Postman, server-to-server HTTP) can ignore CORS headers completely. Always keep authentication and authorization on your API endpoints regardless of CORS settings.

data.title: Program.cs — Correct Middleware Order
data.content: Place CORS in the right order to avoid preflight failures.

data.title: Fix a Broken CORS Configuration
data.description: A developer reports that their frontend cannot call the API. Review and fix the code.
steps: Read the following broken configuration: the API uses AllowAnyOrigin() together with AllowCredentials().
Identify why this causes a CORS error in the browser.
Rewrite the policy to use WithOrigins("https://trusted.example.com") and AllowCredentials().
Move UseCors to the correct position in the middleware pipeline.
data.expectedOutcome: A corrected CORS configuration that works in production without runtime errors.

items.text: I know why AllowAnyOrigin and AllowCredentials should never be used together
I can read a CORS error and match it to a fix
I understand that CORS is a browser-side mechanism, not a server-side security boundary
I can place UseCors in the correct middleware order

data.title: Module Summary
points: CORS relaxes the same-origin policy so trusted frontends can call your API
Use named policies for maintainable, reusable rules
Preflight OPTIONS requests are handled automatically by ASP.NET Core middleware
Always pair AllowCredentials with explicit origins, not wildcards
CORS is not a replacement for authentication and authorization
data.takeaway: You now have the full picture: from same-origin basics to production-ready CORS configuration in ASP.NET Core.
